worksheet.title: Plan Your Algorithm
worksheet.subtitle: Plan it, write it, then make it better
worksheet.learning_goal: I can plan and write my own algorithm, then improve it.

parts.title: You are the coder
parts.text: Plan an algorithm: think of the steps, write them in order, then check by doing it in your head. Two jobs to plan — a pattern and a real task — then make one better.

parts.title: Plan a pattern
parts.prompt: Plan a pattern of 6 shapes using ● and ■. Write your steps (box 1 → draw ?, box 2 → draw ?, …), then draw your pattern in the boxes above.

parts.title: Plan a real job
parts.prompt: Pick a job you know — pack your backpack, make a snack, or get ready for school. Write the steps in order (4 to 6 steps), one per line.

parts.title: Make it better
parts.prompt: Read your job algorithm. Add ONE step, or fix the order, to make it better. Write your change and tell why it helps.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: You can read, write, follow, and plan algorithms — and make them better. That is what coders do every day. You are a coder!

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: The unit finale: students plan and write a full set of steps for a pattern and for a real task, then improve one by adding a step or fixing the order. Read, write, and improve a plan — all on one page. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: cut the steps into cards so students can physically slide them into order before writing.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20–25 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Plan a 6-shape pattern by writing what goes in each box, then drawing it.
2. Do one together. Start a task plan together (e.g. pack your backpack) — steps in order.
3. Let them try. Students finish their task plan, then improve it by adding a step or fixing the order.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — open; a sample is circle, square, square, circle, square, square. Accept any pattern where the steps match the drawing.
Exercise 2 — open; a sample (pack your backpack): open the backpack, put in your books, put in your lunch, zip it up, put it on. Accept any 4–6 ordered steps.
Exercise 3 — open; a sample improvement: add "check your homework is in" before "zip it up". Accept any added step or reorder with a reason.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: a drawing that does not match the written steps. Check each step against each box.
Make it easier: let them reuse a task from an earlier sheet.
Make it harder: ask them to write a plan with one flexible pair of steps.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students put step-by-step instructions in the right order to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a set of steps, change or reorder one, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child writes a working plan for both the pattern and the task and improves one with a reason.
